where ai fits

About half of a seller's week isn't selling.

It's reading, looking things up, writing the same email a slightly different way, and typing into your CRM. That half is what we're going after today.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Ask for a show of hands: who spent more than an hour yesterday on research, drafting, or CRM updates? Everybody. That's the target. We are not replacing the part where you build trust and read a room. We're buying that part more hours.

where ai fits

What it's good at today, and what it isn't

Good at

Reading and summarizing

A 10-K, forty job postings, a two-hour transcript. Faster than you, and it doesn't get tired. It does miss things, which is why the sources matter.

Good at

First drafts and rehearsal

Email, follow-ups, proposals, and playing the skeptical buyer so you can practice.

Not yet

Knowing your buyer

It has never met them. It doesn't know what was said at the last QBR unless you tell it.

Not yet

Judgment and relationships

When to push, when to walk, who actually signs. That's still you, and it's the paid part.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Keep this honest. The tools are good at volume and language. They are bad at truth they haven't been given and at judgment. Think of a very well-read new hire on their first day: eager, fast, and knows nothing about your accounts until you tell them. Everything we do today is about telling them.

where ai fits

You probably already own the tools

  • A general assistant: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot. One is plenty. Use the paid company seat
  • A meeting recorder: your meeting recorder, or the one built into your video calls
  • Your CRM's assistant: your CRM ships one now. It's fine for notes and summaries
  • Enrichment and sequencing: your sequencer for the lists and sends. Keep the AI in the drafting seat
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Resist the urge to buy anything this quarter. The general assistant plus a recorder gets you ninety percent of what we'll cover. The CRM copilots are good at the boring parts, which is exactly where you want them. Tool shopping is procrastination with a budget.

01

Set it up once

Three short files turn a generic chatbot into something that knows how you sell.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
This is the module people skip, and it's the one that makes everything else work. Twenty minutes, once.

the three files

Three files your assistant reads before every task

Voice

How you actually write

Five emails you were proud of. Three you'd never send. A line about how you talk to your buyers.

ICP

Who buys, who doesn't

Company size, titles, the trigger events that make them call, and what disqualifies a lead on sight.

Product

your product in the buyer's words

What it does, the three problems it fixes, proof you can name, and what you're not allowed to promise.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Plain text, each under a page. Keep them in whatever your assistant calls a project or a folder, so they load automatically. The voice file is the one people underestimate. Give it your real emails and it stops sounding like a brochure. The ICP file is what makes research and list-ranking useful. The product file keeps it from inventing features.

briefing

Brief it like a new hire, not like a search box

prompt · copy this
You're helping me, an account executive at your company. We sell your product to your buyers.
Read my voice, ICP and product files first.

Task: [what you want, in one sentence]
Who it's for: [name, title, company, what you know about them]
What good looks like: [length, tone, the one ask]
Don't: [anything you'd be embarrassed by]
Before you write, ask me up to three questions if anything is unclear.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Five lines. Who you are, who it's for, what you want, what good looks like, what to avoid. Then the magic line: ask me questions first. A new hire who asks three good questions before starting beats one who guesses. Same here. Have everyone paste this into their assistant now and fill in the brackets for a real account.

briefing

Three habits that fix most bad answers

  • Give it the source material. Paste the page, the transcript, the job post. Don't make it guess
  • Ask for three options, then pick and refine one. Never accept the first draft
  • Tell it what to check. "Flag anything you're not sure is true" works better than hoping
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Most complaints about these tools come down to under-briefing. People type nine words and get a generic answer, then decide it doesn't work. Feed it, ask for options, make it show its doubts. That's it. Demo one bad prompt and one good prompt live if time allows.

exercise · 6 minutes

Build your voice file right now

prompt · copy this
Here are five emails I've sent that I think are good, and three I'd never send.
[paste them]
Write a one-page style guide for writing as me: sentence length, how I open and close,
words I use, words I never use, how formal I am with your buyers.
Then draft a two-line test email in my voice so I can check it.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Six minutes. Phones away, open the sent folder, find five. If they can't find five they're proud of, three is fine. Walk the room. The test email at the end is the check: if it doesn't sound like them, they tell it what's off and run it again. Save the result as voice.md.

02

Research an account in ten minutes

The brief you'd want before any first call, with links, from a company name.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
This is the fastest payback in the whole session. Most reps either skip research or spend an hour on it. Ten minutes, every time, is the goal.

research

Collect, brief, verify, then one sentence on why now

01

Collect

Their site, latest news, open job postings, the annual report if public, and the LinkedIn pages for your two or three contacts.

>
02

Brief

One prompt, with your ICP and product files loaded, produces the page.

>
03

Verify

Every claim gets a link. No link, no claim. Fix the two things it got wrong.

>
04

Why now

One line you could say out loud: the trigger, the likely pain, your angle.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Collect is where most of the ten minutes goes, and it's mostly copy and paste. If your assistant can browse, let it, but still paste the job postings. Hiring is the best public signal of what a company is about to do. Verify is non-negotiable. The brief is a draft, not a fact sheet, until you've clicked the links.

research · the prompt

The account brief prompt

prompt · copy this
Build a one-page account brief on [Company]. Use my ICP and product files.
Sources attached: [paste or link site, news, job posts, filings, contact profiles].

Sections: what they do and how they make money; what changed in the last six months;
what they're hiring for and what that says; who my contacts are and what they care about;
where your product plausibly fits, in their words; three discovery questions; one "why now" sentence.
Cite a source for every factual claim. If you can't source it, mark it UNVERIFIED.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Read the last line out loud. UNVERIFIED in capital letters is the whole trick. The model will tell you what it's unsure of if you give it permission. Then the brief becomes a to-do list for your own checking instead of a trap.

research · what to check

Four things it gets wrong, and how you catch them

  • Stale people. Titles change. Check the two contacts on LinkedIn before you mention them
  • Look-alike companies. Two firms with similar names get blended. Confirm the domain
  • Invented numbers and quotes. If you can't click to it, it didn't happen
  • Trigger events that are old news. Check the date on anything it calls recent
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
These four cover almost every embarrassing research mistake I've seen. They take ninety seconds to check and they are the difference between sounding prepared and sounding like you used a bot. Which is exactly what the buyer is listening for right now.

exercise · 8 minutes

Pick a real target account and run it

  • Choose an account you're actually working. Not a famous one, one of yours
  • Collect for four minutes, run the prompt, read the brief
  • Click two links. Fix what's wrong. Write the "why now" sentence in your own words
  • We'll hear three "why now" sentences from the room
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Eight minutes with a timer on the screen. Walk the room and look for people stuck on Collect; help them grab the job postings. The debrief is the "why now" sentences. Push back gently on vague ones. If it isn't something you'd say on a call, it isn't done.

03

Outreach that sounds like you

Short, specific, one ask, and nothing goes out you didn't read.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Everyone in the room has received AI-written outreach this week. They can smell it. The goal is the opposite: email that reads like a person who did ten minutes of homework.

outreach

Personalization isn't their name in the first line. It's proof you did the ten minutes.

The trigger sentence from your brief is the personalization. Everything else is just polite.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
"Hi Sarah, I saw you're the VP of Platform at Acme" is not personalization. It's mail merge. "Your team posted four Kubernetes roles last month" is. The research module feeds this one directly.

outreach · the first touch

Under ninety words, one ask, an easy out

prompt · copy this
Using my voice file and the account brief for [Company], write a first-touch email to [Name, Title].
Rules: under 90 words, plain text, no bullet points, no buzzwords.
Open with the trigger from the brief in one sentence. Ask one plain question about what they're
trying to solve. Offer the docs or 20 minutes, their choice. Close with a line that makes it easy
to say no. Give me three versions with different openings.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Ninety words is a real constraint and the model respects it. The easy out matters: "if this isn't on your radar, tell me and I'll stop" gets replies because it costs the reader nothing. Three versions, then you pick and tune. Never the first draft.

outreach · before and after

The same email, before and after the brief

Before, from a cold template

Hi Sarah, I hope this finds you well. I'm reaching out because your company helps organizations like yours unlock value with your product. Leading companies trust us to drive outcomes. I'd love to find 30 minutes to share how we can help Acme accelerate its journey. Are you free next week?

After, from the brief and the voice file

Sarah, your team posted four platform roles last month, which usually means the Kubernetes footprint just got bigger than one person can watch. What are you trying to fix first with it?

Happy to point you at the right docs, or 20 minutes if talking is easier. If it's not on your radar, say so and I'll stop.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Read both out loud. The left one could have been sent by any company to any company. The right one proves homework in the first sentence, asks one real question, and makes "no" a free answer. Say up front that the left one was written to be bad on purpose; every phrase in it is from a real vendor email. Same model wrote both. The difference is what it was given.

outreach · sequences

What to automate in your sequencer and what stays in your hands

  • Three emails, same thread, days 0, 3 and 8. The last one asks if you should close it out
  • LinkedIn stays a manual task. Automating connection requests gets your account restricted
  • Stops on reply, meeting, bounce, unsubscribe, or an opportunity. Nurture pauses while they're in it
  • The AI drafts every step. You approve the first send to each person
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
This is the sequence shape I use. Email can be automated once the drafts are approved, and every automated send carries a working unsubscribe and your postal address; your sequencer handles both if the template is set up right. LinkedIn cannot be automated, and it's not a style choice; the platform restricts the member's account for it. The approval on first send is the human gate. Later, when the reply and complaint numbers look healthy, loosen it.

outreach

Nothing goes out that you didn't read. Not because the AI is bad. Because it's your name.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Say it plainly and move on. People remember the short version.

exercise · 8 minutes

Write the first touch for the account you just researched

  • Run the first-touch prompt with your brief and your voice file loaded
  • Pick one of the three. Cut anything you wouldn't say on the phone
  • Read it to the person next to you. They tell you if it sounds like you
  • Count the words. Under ninety or cut again
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
The read-aloud test is the best editor in the room. If they stumble on a phrase, the buyer will too. Collect two volunteers to read theirs and ask the room: would you reply to that?

04

Before, during and after the call

Prep in five minutes, listen instead of typing, follow up before lunch.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
The call is where the relationship happens, so the assistant stays out of the room. It earns its keep on either side of it.

the call

Five minutes before, nothing during, ten minutes after

01

Before

From the brief: five discovery questions, the two objections you'll hear, who's in the room and what each one cares about.

>
02

During

Recorder on, with consent. You look at the person, not the keyboard. Your notes are three words and a star.

>
03

After

Transcript in, out comes the summary, the follow-up email in your voice, the CRM notes, the tasks with dates.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Ask for consent on recording every time; most teams already do. The "during" box is the point: the best sellers in the room already don't take notes. Now nobody has to. After the call, ten minutes, before you open the next tab, or the follow-up slides to tomorrow and the energy is gone.

the call · prep

The prep sheet prompt

prompt · copy this
Using the account brief for [Company] and my product file, prepare me for a 30-minute discovery call
with [names and titles]. Give me: five open questions in the order I'd ask them; the two objections
I'm most likely to hear and a one-line honest answer to each; what each person in the room probably
cares about; the two technical terms from the brief I should be able to explain in one sentence;
one thing I should not bring up yet. Keep it to one page I can read in five minutes.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
"One thing I should not bring up yet" is my favorite line in this prompt. Pricing, a competitor, a feature that isn't shipped. The model is good at spotting the landmine when you ask. The two technical terms line is for anyone selling to engineers: if you can't explain the buyer's words in one sentence, they'll know in the first five minutes.

the call · rehearsal

Rehearse the hard conversation before you have it

prompt · copy this
Play [Name], [Title] at [Company]. You're skeptical, busy, and you've been burned by a vendor
like us before. Use the account brief for what you know and care about. I'll pitch and handle
objections; you push back the way a real buyer would, one message at a time. Don't go easy on me.
After ten exchanges, stop and tell me the three weakest things I said and what to say instead.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Nobody wants to role-play with their manager. Everyone will do it with a chatbot at eleven at night. The feedback at the end is honest in a way colleagues rarely are. Managers: this is your new ride-along.

the call · follow-up

Follow up in ten minutes from the transcript

prompt · copy this
Here's the transcript of my call with [Company]. [paste]
Produce four things: a 5-line summary in my words; a follow-up email in my voice that restates what
they said they need, confirms the next step and date, and asks nothing new; CRM notes under
"Pain, Timeline, Budget, Decision process, Competition, Next step"; and a task list with owners
and dates. Flag anything they said that contradicts our account brief.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
The structure for CRM notes is whatever your team uses. Change the six headings to match your CRM. The contradiction flag at the end is the quiet win: it catches the moment the buyer told you something that changes the deal and you were too busy listening to write it down.

exercise · 6 minutes

Three rounds with your toughest buyer

  • Run the rehearsal prompt against the account you've been using all session
  • Ten exchanges, then read the three weakest things it caught
  • Tell the table the one you're going to fix before your next real call
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Keep it to six minutes. People get into this one. The debrief question is the useful part: name the fix. If you want a bigger version of this, pair people up and have one person's assistant play the buyer while the other pitches live.

05

Proposals and the paperwork

The words around the numbers get written for you. The numbers are still yours.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Proposals and RFPs are where sellers lose evenings. This is the module that gives them back, with one hard rule about numbers.

proposals

First draft from your template and the call

prompt · copy this
Using our proposal template [paste], my product file, and the transcript and notes from [Company] [paste],
draft the proposal. Restate their problem in their own words from the transcript. Map each need to
what your product does, with the proof we can name. Leave every price, discount, and date as [TBD]
for me to fill in. Add a mutual action plan with the steps between today and signature.
Flag any promise in the draft that isn't in my product file.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Two protections are built in. Prices and dates stay as TBD so the model never invents a number that ends up in front of a buyer. And the last line catches the thing proposals are famous for: a promise that sales made and the product doesn't keep. Read every flag.

proposals

The same move works for RFPs and the business case

  • RFPs: keep your past answers in a file. It drafts new answers from old ones and marks the gaps
  • Business case: give it their numbers from the call and ask for the math shown step by step
  • Executive summary: ask for one paragraph a CFO would read, then one a CTO would read
  • Every number gets checked by a human before it leaves the building. No exceptions
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
The RFP library is a real asset once you have it. Twenty answered RFPs in a folder and the next one is a day's work instead of a week's. The business case: insist on shown math. If it can't show the arithmetic, it made the number up.

06

Keep the pipeline honest

CRM notes that write themselves, and a second opinion on every deal.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
This is the module for anyone who has ever updated your CRM at 4:55 on a Friday. Also the one managers like most.

pipeline · deal review

Ask it to be the skeptic in your deal review

prompt · copy this
Here are my notes, emails and call summaries for the [Company] deal. [paste]
Act as a tough sales manager. Tell me: what we actually know versus what I'm assuming; who the real
decision maker is and whether I've talked to them; what could kill this deal in the next 30 days;
the one action that most improves our odds this week. Be blunt. Don't tell me what I want to hear.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
People find this uncomfortable and then they run it on every deal. It is very good at spotting the deal that's all enthusiasm and no economic buyer. Run it before the pipeline review, not after, so you walk in with the answer.

pipeline · hygiene

Hygiene without the Friday afternoon

  • CRM notes come out of the follow-up prompt. Paste them in while the email sends
  • Weekly summary: paste the week's notes, ask for wins, risks, asks, and what you need from your manager
  • Forecast commentary: ask for the one-line reason behind every stage change
  • If the CRM has its own assistant, let it do the summaries. Keep the thinking in yours
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
The weekly summary prompt takes two minutes and makes your manager's week easier, which is a career move dressed up as hygiene. Point at the fourth line: CRM copilots are good at structured summaries. The judgment prompts belong in your general assistant with your three files loaded.

07

The rules that keep you employed

Four of them. None are complicated.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Short module, serious tone. These aren't legal boilerplate. Every one of them is a story I've watched happen to someone.

guardrails

Four rules

01

Some things never go in

Customer confidential data, personal data beyond a name and title, unreleased pricing or roadmap. Unless your company's tool is approved for it, it stays out.

02

Use the company seat

The team or business account has the retention and training settings your admin set. Your personal login doesn't.

03

Check before you trust

Names, numbers, dates, quotes. If you'd be embarrassed to be wrong about it, click the source.

04

It never sends

A working unsubscribe and your postal address on every sequence, by law. The assistant drafts. A person reads and sends.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Rule one is the one people break by accident, usually by pasting a whole transcript with a customer's architecture in it into a free consumer tool. Ask your security team which tool is approved and what can go in it. Rule two is the fix for most of rule one. Rule four has a legal half: every commercial email needs a working unsubscribe and a real postal address, and the sequencer handles both if the template is set up right. Check with ops before the first send. The other half you've heard all session.

guardrails

At 99 percent accuracy, a thousand automated sends is ten mistakes with your signature on them.

Errors compound at machine speed. The human gate is the circuit breaker.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
This is why the one rule exists. I'm not claiming models are 99 percent accurate; even if they were, the math still gets you. A model that's right 99 times out of 100 feels perfect in a demo. Run it unattended across a thousand contacts and the ten bad ones are the ones that get forwarded. Keep the person in the loop where the name goes on it.

08

Your first week

One workflow, every day, for two weeks. Then add the next one.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Don't try to do all of this Monday. Pick one. The research brief is the usual winner because it pays off on the very first call.

your first week

Five days, one habit each

Day 1
Build the three files
Voice, ICP, product. Twenty minutes. Save them where your assistant loads them automatically.
Day 2
Brief three accounts
Ten minutes each. Click the links. Write the "why now" sentence for each.
Day 3
Rewrite one sequence
Three emails, under ninety words each, in your voice. Approve the first send yourself.
Day 4
Record one call
Prep sheet before, recorder on, follow-up and CRM notes sent inside ten minutes.
Day 5
Review your toughest deal
Run the skeptic prompt. Take the one action it names.
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Point, don't read. Each day is a module from today. By Friday they've done every workflow once on real accounts. Then they pick the one that paid off most and make it daily.

your first week · measure

Measure three things, nothing fancy

  • Hours back per week. Guess honestly on Friday afternoon
  • Reply rate on the rewritten sequence against the old one
  • Follow-ups sent the same day, as a percentage of calls
// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Three numbers on a sticky note. If hours back isn't at least three after two weeks, something's wrong with the setup, usually the three files. If the reply rate didn't move, the trigger line isn't landing. Same-day follow-ups is the one managers should watch.

your first week

Pick one workflow. Do it every day for two weeks. Then add the next.

// AI for Sales Professionals
PERIPETY LABS
Last word before the close. The people who get value from this are the ones who make one thing a habit. The ones who try everything on Monday are back to the old way by Thursday.
